keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Each place is ten times the place to its right. 10 ones make 1 ten. 10 tens make 1 hundred. 10 hundreds make 1 thousand. And now — 10 thousands make 1 ten-thousand . The same pattern keeps the chart growing. In 27,438, the 2 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 20,000 . The 7 right next to it is worth 7,000. Same digit, very different value — the place decides. 🔗 27,438 — Four Ways to Show the Same Number You just built 27,438 with discs. Look at the same number shown four different ways. keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Three strategies for adding multi-digit numbers. 1. Make a Friendly Number. Bump one addend up or down to a clean 100, 1,000, or 5,000. Do the easy addition. At the end, take back what you added (or add back what you took away). Best when one number is within 5 of a friendly value. 2. Decompose by Place. Split each number into thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. Add place by place. Best when the place values are already clean (lots of zeros). 3. Standard Algorithm. Stack, add, carry. Always works. Use when the other two don't fit. Cora's rule: estimate FIRST. Then check that your strategy's answer is close to your estimate. If they're far apart, you lost track somewhere. 🎯 Watch a Friendly Bump Live: 2,997 + 4,128 Step through Felix's compensation move.
⚖️ Head-to-Head Comparison 🎯 MAKE FRIENDLY 4,998 + 2,375 = (5,000 + 2,375) − 2 = 7,375 − 2 = 7,373 3 steps · 0 carries
lesson.missionQuestion: When does the standard algorithm win, and when does a mental strategy win?
objectives: Make a friendly number by rounding one addend up or down, then adjusting.
Use compensation — add a little extra to make the math easier, then take it back.
Choose the best strategy for the numbers in front of you — algorithm, mental, or break-apart.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.

planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

items.title: Lesson 02.03: Other Ways to Add and Subtract – Part 1

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Three strategies for subtracting multi-digit numbers. 1. Equal Change. Add (or subtract) the same amount to BOTH numbers. The difference doesn't change. Best when the subtrahend (the bottom number) is close to a friendly value. 2. Count Up. Start at the smaller number. Count up — friendly jumps first — to the bigger number. The total you counted is the difference. Best when there's a clean route between the numbers. 3. Standard Algorithm. Stack, regroup, subtract. Always works. Use when the other two don't fit. Why equal change works: a subtraction is a GAP between two numbers. If you slide BOTH numbers the same distance, the gap doesn't move. ⬆️ Watch a Count-Up Live: 5,003 − 1,998 Step through Felix's jumps to friendly numbers.
⚖️ Head-to-Head Comparison ⚖️ EQUAL CHANGE 6,005 − 2,997 add 3 to both = 6,008 − 3,000 = 3,008 3 steps · 0 regroups
lesson.missionQuestion: If adding the same amount to BOTH numbers in a subtraction doesn't change the difference, why is that true?
objectives: Count up from the smaller number to the bigger one — the difference is what you counted.
Use equal change — add (or subtract) the same amount to BOTH numbers to dodge regrouping.
Choose the best subtraction strategy — algorithm, count up, or equal change — by reading the numbers first.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.lessonTitle: Other Ways to Add and Subtract - Part 2
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

items.title: Lesson 02.04: Other Ways to Add and Subtract – Part 2

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Two bar shapes for every word problem. 1. Part-Part-Whole. One long bar split into two parts. If the WHOLE is missing → add the parts. If one PART is missing → subtract the known part from the whole. 2. Comparison. Two bars stacked side by side. The GAP between them is "how many more" or "how many fewer." Always subtract (bigger minus smaller). The bar shape is what you draw FIRST. Once the bar is drawn, the operation appears — you can SEE the missing piece. 🔁 Two-Step Story: First Bar, Then Another Walk through a story that needs TWO bars and TWO operations.

⚖️ The Word Problem Method Step 1 — Read. Read the story TWICE. What is happening? What is missing? Step 2 — Draw. Part-Part-Whole or Comparison? Sketch the bar. Step 3 — Operation. Bar shape tells you. Combining parts → add. Missing part / compare → subtract. Step 4 — Strategy. Algorithm, Make Friendly, Decompose, Count Up, Equal Change — whichever fits the numbers. Step 5 — Check. Estimate first. Plug answer back into story. Does it make sense?
lesson.missionQuestion: When a word problem doesn't tell you which operation to use, how do you decide?
objectives: Draw a bar model for any addition or subtraction word problem — part-part-whole or comparison.
Solve two-step problems by working out one bar first, then using its answer in the next.
Choose the best strategy from your full toolkit — algorithm, Make Friendly, Decompose, Count Up, or Equal Change.

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Three equivalent definitions of "multiple." A number is a multiple of 4 if (all three mean the same thing): 1. You land on it when you skip count by 4 (starting at 4). 2. You can make it by multiplying 4 by some whole number — 4 × 1, 4 × 2, 4 × 3, etc. 3. It divides evenly by 4 — no remainder. These are not three different things. They are three views of the SAME family of numbers. ⬜ Picture It: Multiples as Arrays See multiples as rectangles of dots.
lesson.missionQuestion: What does it mean for a number to be a "multiple" of another number?
objectives: List the first ten multiples of any one-digit number using skip counting.
Decide whether a given number is or is NOT a multiple of another (use division or skip counting).
Explain the connection between multiples, skip counting, and the multiplication table.

planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw Two methods for finding the LCM of two numbers. 1. List and scan. List the first 5-10 multiples of each number. Scan for the FIRST number that appears in BOTH lists. That's the LCM. Always works. 2. Product shortcut (sometimes). When two numbers share NO common factor (like 3 and 5, or 7 and 8), the LCM equals their product. 3 × 5 = 15 = LCM. Doesn't work when they share a factor — then you have to list. Big idea: a common multiple is a number that lives in BOTH lists. The LCM is the smallest one. Common multiples solve "when do two repeating events line up" problems. ⭕ Picture It: The Venn Diagram Two circles. The overlap holds the common multiples.
⚖️ When Does the Product Shortcut Work? ✅ Shortcut WORKS When the two numbers share no factor besides 1. LCM(3, 5) = 3 × 5 = 15 ✓ LCM(7, 4) = 7 × 4 = 28 ✓ LCM(9, 2) = 9 × 2 = 18 ✓
lesson.missionQuestion: Common multiples solve real problems: when will two events that repeat on different rhythms line up again?
objectives: List multiples of two numbers and circle the ones that appear in BOTH lists.
Find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) — the smallest number both lists share.
Apply common multiples to story problems (events repeating on different schedules).

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw How to find EVERY factor of a number — systematically. 1. Start at 1. Every whole number has 1 as a factor (and the number itself). Write down 1 × number . 2. Try each whole number in order. 2, 3, 4, 5… Divide. If no remainder, you've found a factor PAIR — that divisor AND its quotient. 3. Stop when the divisor equals or passes its partner. If 24 ÷ 5 doesn't work and you've already found pairs up to 4 × 6, you're done — every smaller number has been checked. Factors come in pairs. Every "yes" gives you TWO factors at once. The factor list is finite — you can't miss any if you go in order. ▭ Picture It: Every Rectangle = One Factor Pair Hazel's rectangle method, applied to 12.
⚖️ Factors of 36 Pair Multiplication 1 and 36 1 × 36 = 36 2 and 18 2 × 18 = 36 3 and 12 3 × 12 = 36 4 and 9 4 × 9 = 36 6 and 6 6 × 6 = 36 (square!)
lesson.missionQuestion: If multiples are the family a number BELONGS to, what are factors?
objectives: List all factor pairs of a given number by trying division systematically (1, 2, 3, 4…).
Decide whether one number IS or IS NOT a factor of another (Cora's no-remainder rule).
Explain why every factor comes with a paired factor — and when to stop searching.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw The prime/composite definitions and how to test fast. 1. Prime: exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. 2. Composite: more than 2 factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18. 3. 1 is neither. Only one factor (itself). Not "exactly 2" → not prime. Not "more than 2" → not composite. Quick tests (divisibility): divisible by 2 if even; by 3 if digit sum divides by 3; by 5 if ends in 0 or 5. To test a number under 100, check 2, 3, 5, and 7. None divide → prime. 🌟 Picture It: The First 25 Primes A handy reference for the rest of the unit.

⚠️ Sneaky Composites (Look Prime, Aren't) These numbers are ODD (so they look prime) but are actually COMPOSITE. Memorize them. 9 = 3×3 15 = 3×5 21 = 3×7 25 = 5×5 27 = 3×9 33 = 3×11 35 = 5×7 39 = 3×13 49 = 7×7 51 = 3×17 55 = 5×11 63 = 7×9
lesson.missionQuestion: Why does a "shortest possible factor list" make some numbers special?
objectives: Define prime (exactly 2 factors) and composite (more than 2 factors).
Test any number under 100 to decide whether it's prime or composite.
Explain why 1 is treated as its own special case — neither prime nor composite.

items.title: Lesson 03.04: Prime Numbers and Composite Numbers

keyConcepts: 📐 What You Just Saw How to find the GCF of two numbers. 1. List factors of each number (use yesterday's systematic search). 2. Circle the numbers that appear in BOTH lists — those are the common factors. 3. The biggest one is the GCF. Shortcuts to know: If one number divides the other (like 6 and 18), the GCF is the smaller one (6). keyConcepts: 📐 Three Mental Multiplication Tools 1. Decompose by place. Break a multi-digit factor into place pieces. Multiply each piece. Add the parts. Example: 47 × 5 = (40 × 5) + (7 × 5) = 200 + 35 = 235. 2. Times-ten patterns. Tack zeros onto a factor → tack the SAME number of zeros onto the product. Example: 8 × 5 = 40. So 80 × 5 = 400. And 800 × 5 = 4,000. 3. Compensate. Round one factor to a friendly number, multiply, then adjust. Example: 199 × 4 = (200 × 4) − 4 = 800 − 4 = 796. 🧱 Picture It: Area Model for 23 × 4 See the place-value split as a real rectangle.

⚖️ Compensation Step-by-Step Original problem: 5 × $4,999 Step 1. Bump 4,999 UP to 5,000 (added 1 to each frame's price). Step 2. Easy product: 5 × 5,000 = $25,000 . Step 3. Take back: bumped 1 per frame, 5 frames → 5 extra dollars. $25,000 − $5 = $24,995 . Final answer: $24,995.
objectives: Multiply by 10, 100, and 1,000 by shifting digits — no algorithm needed.
Decompose a number by place value to multiply (12 × 3 = 10 × 3 + 2 × 3).

keyConcepts: 📐 The Column Algorithm, Step by Step For any multi-digit × 1-digit multiplication: 1. Stack the multi-digit number on top, the 1-digit factor below. Line them up at the ones place. 2. Multiply right to left. Start at the ones column. Multiply the bottom digit by the top digit in that column. 3. Carry when needed. If a column product is 10 or more, write the ones digit and CARRY the tens digit to the next column. 4. Add carries. When you multiply the next column, ADD any carry from the previous column to the product. 5. Continue. Move left one column at a time until done. Write the full product below the line. ▭ Picture It: Area Model for 3,521 × 3 Hazel's decomposition view of the same product.
⚖️ Two Estimates vs. the Exact Round to 1,000 5,000 × 4 = 20,000 off by 688
lesson.missionQuestion: If decomposition SHOWS why multiplication works, how does the column algorithm DO the same thing with less writing?
objectives: Estimate any product by rounding one factor to a friendly number.
Use an area model to multiply a multi-digit number by a one-digit number.

keyConcepts: 📐 Chained Carries — Stay Organized When carries chain across many columns: 1. Write each carry SMALL above the next column. Use a different color or just a tiny number. Don't skip this — chained carries get lost fast. 2. ADD the carry to the next column's product. Compute the bottom × top first, THEN add the carry. 3. Cross out each carry once you use it. So you don't add it twice. 4. Sanity-check with the estimate. If your exact is way off your estimate, slow down and find the missed (or doubled) carry. 📏 Rough vs. Tight Estimates When to use each kind.

⚖️ Estimate-Driven Reasoning Question: Is 9,183 × 3 above or below 25,000? Estimate: 9,000 × 3 = 27,000. Reasoning: 9,183 > 9,000, so 9,183 × 3 > 27,000 > 25,000. Verified: 9,183 × 3 = 27,549. ✓ Above 25,000. When a question asks "above or below?", you usually don't need the exact answer — a careful estimate gives you the decision.
objectives: Choose the right rounding place for the estimate you need (rough vs. tight).
Multiply 5-digit numbers by a 1-digit factor using the column algorithm.

keyConcepts: 📐 Three Mental Division Tools 1. Number bonds. Split the dividend into two pieces that BOTH divide evenly. Divide each piece. Add the quotients. keyConcepts: 📐 The Lead-Digit Trick To predict the number of digits in a quotient: 1. Compare the dividend's FIRST digit to the divisor. 2. If first digit ≥ divisor , the quotient has AS MANY digits as the dividend. Example: 9,875 ÷ 4. First digit 9 ≥ 4 → quotient has 4 digits. 3. If first digit < divisor , the quotient has ONE FEWER digit. Example: 7,489 ÷ 8. First digit 7 < 8 → quotient has 3 digits. This catches "missing place" errors fast. If your long-division answer has the wrong number of digits, you missed a step. 🔍 Sofia, Mei, Dion — Three Estimates of 4,975 ÷ 3 Same setup as 4.05.02, now with bigger numbers.

keyConcepts: 📐 The Two Rules for Equivalent Fractions Rule 1 — Build equivalents (×n/n): Multiply the numerator AND the denominator by the SAME number. The value stays the same. a/b = (a × n) / (b × n) Example: 2 3 × 4 4 = 8 12 Rule 2 — Simplify (÷n/n): Divide the numerator AND the denominator by the SAME number (usually a common factor). The value stays the same. a/b = (a ÷ n) / (b ÷ n) Example: 8 12 ÷ 4 4 = 2 3 Why both rules work: You're really multiplying or dividing the fraction by 1 (because n/n = 1). 1 doesn't change the value — it just changes how the pie LOOKS. 🥧 Picture It: The ×n/n Family One fraction. Many equivalents. Same shaded amount.
⚖️ Three Ways to See an Equivalent PIE / BAR The shaded area is the SAME. Different cuts. 1 2 = 4 8 (same pie)

keyConcepts: 📐 Three Ways to Compare Fractions Way 1 — Same denominator: If the denominators MATCH, compare the numerators. Bigger top = bigger fraction. ( 5 12 vs 7 12 → 7 12 wins.) Rename, then compare Way 3 — Benchmark to 1 2 or 1: Is each fraction more or less than 1 2 ? If one is more and one is less, the answer is instant. ( 3 5 vs 4 9 → 3 5 is more than 1 2 , 4 9 is less, so 3 5 wins.) Why all three work: A fraction names a single position on the number line. Comparing two fractions just means asking which position is farther right. 📊 Picture It: Ordering on the Number Line Three fractions. One number line. Smallest to largest.

keyConcepts: 📐 Improper Fractions vs Mixed Numbers Improper fraction: top number is BIGGER than (or equal to) the bottom. It tells you how many slices of size 1/denominator you have — even if that's more than a whole pie. 8 5 = "eight one-fifth slices" Mixed number: a whole number AND a fraction together. Whole part = how many full pies. Fraction part = how much of one more pie. 1 3 5 = "one whole pie and three more fifths" Same amount, two outfits: 8 5 = 1 3/5. You can prove it by counting slices both ways — 5 in the whole + 3 leftover = 8 total. ✓ How to tell which is more than 1: compare top and bottom of an improper. If top > bottom → more than 1 whole. If top = bottom → exactly 1. If top < bottom → less than 1 (it's a proper fraction). 🥧 Picture It: Same Spot, Two Names Pies on the left. Number line on the right. Two ways to name the same amount.

keyConcepts: 📐 The Two Rules Perimeter = add every side once = length + width + length + width. Shortcut for rectangles: P = 2 × (L + W). For a SQUARE: P = 4 × side. Answer is in LINEAR units (cm, m, ft, in) — not square units. 📐 Picture It: Working Backward from Perimeter If you know the perimeter and one side, find the other.
🚶 Lesson 11.04 in One Image Perimeter = sum of all sides. Rectangle: 2 × (L + W). Square: 4 × side. Missing side from perimeter? Subtract knowns, then divide by 2 (or by 4 for a square).
lesson.missionQuestion: How can you tell?
objectives: Read an improper fraction like 8 5 and shade pies to match.
Interpret a fraction as equal sharing (2 pies ÷ 5 students = 2 5 each).
Simplify the fraction part when the result can be reduced (e.g., 6 4 → 1 1 2 ).

keyConcepts: 📐 The Composite Perimeter Rule Label every side first. Find any missing sides by subtracting the known pieces from the full length. Then add every side exactly once. For L-shapes, T-shapes, and stairs, the perimeter equals the perimeter of the outer bounding rectangle. 📐 Picture It: Why the Notch Doesn't Change the Perimeter The L-shape and its bounding rectangle have the same perimeter.
📐 Lesson 11.05 in One Image Label every side first. Then sum them all once. For an L-shape: perimeter equals the outer bounding rectangle's perimeter.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you find the perimeter of an L-shape or T-shape when some sides aren't labeled?
objectives: Find missing sides on a composite figure by subtracting from the outer dimensions.
Label every side of an L-shape, T-shape, or stairs, going clockwise.
Sum all sides exactly once to find the perimeter.

info.label: Focus
info.value: Read and write tenths as fractions and decimals

keyConcepts: 📐 Two Ways to Write a Tenth Fraction form: count of shaded pieces OVER 10. (3/10, 5/10, 7/10.) Decimal form: the SAME count of pieces written after a decimal point. (0.3, 0.5, 0.7.) Same number. Two notations. Choose whichever fits the situation. 📐 Picture It: Three Ways to See 0.3 Strip, number line, fraction. All the same number.
🔟 Lesson 12.01 in One Image A tenth is 1 of 10 equal pieces of a whole. 3 shaded → 3/10 → 0.3. Same number, two notations.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you write three-tenths as a decimal?
objectives: Read tenths from a shaded strip and a number line.
Write a tenth as a fraction (over 10) AND as a decimal (0.n).
Convert between the two notations.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

keyConcepts: 📐 Place-Value Rules for Decimals Decimal point separates ones (left) from tenths (right). Regroup whenever tenths ≥ 10: 10 tenths = 1 one. (Just like 10 ones = 1 ten — same rule, one place to the right.) Expanded form: 2.3 = 2 + 0.3. Each digit times its place value, summed. 📐 Picture It: Decimals in Real Life Measurements use decimals all the time.
📊 Lesson 12.02 in One Image Ones LEFT of the point. Tenths RIGHT. Whenever tenths hit 10, regroup into 1 one.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you write a decimal that is greater than 1?
objectives: Build decimals using a place-value chart (ones + tenths).
Regroup 10 tenths into 1 one when needed.
Decompose a decimal as ones + tenths in expanded form.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

keyConcepts: 📐 Hundredths Rules Two decimal places means hundredths. 0.23 = 23 hundredths = 23/100. 1 tenth = 10 hundredths. So 0.1 = 0.10 (both equal 1 tenth). Adding a trailing zero in the hundredths place doesn't change the value. Leading zero matters! 0.07 (7 hundredths) is very different from 0.7 (7 tenths). 📐 Picture It: 0.3 and 0.30 Are the Same A whole column shaded is 10 hundredths = 1 tenth.
💯 Lesson 12.03 in One Image n hundredths = n/100 = 0.nn (two decimal places). A whole row = 10 hundredths = 1 tenth (0.1 = 0.10).
lesson.missionQuestion: How is it different from a tenth?
objectives: Read hundredths from a 10×10 grid.
Write each amount as a fraction (n/100) AND as a decimal (0.nn).
Connect tenths and hundredths: 1 tenth = 10 hundredths.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

info.label: Focus
info.value: Place value of each digit; expanded form

keyConcepts: 📐 Place Value in Decimals Tens | Ones · Tenths | Hundredths. Each place is 10 times smaller than the one to its left. Expanded form: 75.84 = 70 + 5 + 0.8 + 0.04. Each digit times its place value, summed. Read aloud with "and" for the decimal point: 75.84 = "seventy-five AND eighty-four hundredths." 📐 Picture It: Counting by Hundredths From 4.97 over the bridge to 5.00 and beyond.
🔢 Lesson 12.04 in One Image Each digit's value = digit × place. Expanded form sums all the place values back to the decimal.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you read a decimal with BOTH tenths AND hundredths?
objectives: Find the value of each digit in a decimal.
Decompose a decimal into expanded form: 75.84 = 70 + 5 + 0.8 + 0.04.
Build a decimal from its expanded parts.

planning.evidence: 4-tab lesson: readiness, concept/CPA, systematic practice, 4-6 independent problems.
planning.sources: scope and sequence 1.pdf; Grade 4 math section

info.label: Focus
info.value: Write decimals as fractions in simplest form

keyConcepts: 📐 Two Steps Step 1: Count decimal places. One place → denominator 10. Two places → denominator 100. Step 2: Simplify by dividing top and bottom by their greatest common factor. Three to know: 0.5 = 1/2. 0.25 = 1/4. 0.75 = 3/4. 📐 Picture It: The Three to Memorize Shaded grids prove the equivalences.
✨ Lesson 12.05 in One Image Write over 10 or 100. Then divide top and bottom by the same factor. 0.5 = 1/2. 0.25 = 1/4. 0.75 = 3/4. Memorize these three.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you turn a decimal into a fraction in simplest form?
objectives: Write a decimal as a fraction over 10 or 100.
Simplify the fraction by dividing top and bottom by the same factor.
Recognize common decimal-fraction equivalents: 0.5 = 1/2, 0.25 = 1/4, 0.75 = 3/4.

items.title: Lesson 12.05: Expressing Decimals as a Fraction in Simplest Form

keyConcepts: 📐 The Multiplier Trick Goal: denominator 10 or 100. Then the numerator IS the decimal digits. Multipliers: /2 needs × 5. /4 needs × 25. /5 needs × 2. /20 needs × 5. /25 needs × 4. /50 needs × 2. If the fraction is already /10 or /100, just write the decimal directly. 📐 Picture It: Multiplier Cheat Sheet Which number to use when.
🔄 Lesson 12.06 in One Image Rename to /10 or /100. Numerator becomes the decimal. For mixed numbers, just convert the fraction part.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you turn a fraction into a decimal?
objectives: Rename a fraction with denominator 10 or 100.
Convert the renamed fraction to a decimal directly.
Apply to mixed numbers: 2 and 1/4 → 2.25.

keyConcepts: 📐 Three Comparison Rules 1. Pad with trailing zeros if the decimals have different lengths. 0.7 = 0.70. 2. Walk left to right. Compare digit by digit, starting at the place left of the decimal point. 3. First arguing place wins. As soon as digits differ, that comparison decides the whole number. 📐 Picture It: Aligning to Compare Stack two decimals at the point.
⚖️ Lesson 12.07 in One Image Align points. Pad with zeros. Walk left to right. First arguing place wins. Trailing zeros don't change value.
lesson.missionQuestion: How do you decide which decimal is bigger?
objectives: Compare two decimals using place value.
Pad with trailing zeros when decimals have different lengths.
Order a list of decimals from least to greatest.

info.label: Focus
info.value: Round decimals to tenths or whole

keyConcepts: 📐 Rounding Steps 1. Pick the place. Nearest tenth, nearest whole, nearest hundredth. 2. Find the two neighbors. The "nice" numbers your decimal sits between at that place. 3. Find halfway. Exactly between the neighbors. 4. Pick the closer neighbor. Halfway always rounds UP. 📐 Picture It: The Halfway Mark A number line shows everything at once.
🎯 Lesson 12.08 in One Image Find neighbors → find halfway → pick the closer one. Exactly at halfway → always round UP.
lesson.missionQuestion: Which one is your decimal closer to?
objectives: Find the two neighbors on the number line.
Pick the closer neighbor (round to that one).
Apply the halfway-up rule when needed.

Summative Assessment One at the end of every module, after the final numbered lesson.

Planning-table assessment rule

Modules with more than three numbered lessons receive one concept check near the midpoint. Every module receives a summative assessment at the end.

Three short-module exceptions have no separate concept check: Grade 3 Module 7, Grade 4 Module 9, and Grade 4 Module 17. Follow the placement tables rather than adding an extra assessment to these modules.

Use a “customize once, duplicate many” workflow

Complete the class-wide setup one time before building individual lesson pages. After that, each lesson or assessment requires only a duplicate, the correct item title, and its unique student link.

Phase 1: Create class-ready master templates once

Prepare one master for Independent Practice, one for Concept Checks, and one for Summative Assessments. Keep these master pages unpublished and clearly labeled so they are never assigned directly to students.

1

Make a working copy of each original template

Duplicate the original Goblins Assignment, Goblins Concept Check, and Goblins Summative Assessment templates. Rename the copies MASTER – Goblins Independent Practice, MASTER – Goblins Concept Check, and MASTER – Goblins Summative Assessment. Leave the original templates untouched as backups.

2

Complete all recurring edits on the masters

Add the teacher name, Canvas Inbox or help directions, class-specific wording, and any other information that will stay the same across the course. Replace the visible 000-000 with the class’s six-digit code. Keep the hyphen.

Example Class Code 016-405
3

Finish and protect the master templates

Remove the gray Teacher Setup box and resolve every recurring EDIT ME field. Do not add an assignment student link yet. Leave the green button’s placeholder URL in the master. Save the masters, keep them unpublished, and place them in a clearly labeled teacher-only area if your course design allows.

Phase 2: Duplicate the correct master for each item

The class code, teacher information, and standard directions will already be complete. Teachers should not rebuild or re-customize the page for every lesson.

4

Duplicate, rename, and place the page

Duplicate the matching master. Rename the new Canvas page to match the lesson or assessment code in the planning table. Update only item-specific text that must change, such as the visible assignment title or learning target, then place the page in the location shown in the scope-and-sequence tables below.

5

Add only that item’s Goblins student link

Create or assign the correct item in Goblins and copy its student link. Do not copy a teacher-dashboard or editing link. In the duplicated Canvas page’s HTML, replace only the URL inside the green button’s href="...".

Before: <a href="https://gob.live" ...>
After:  <a href="PASTE-THIS-ITEMS-STUDENT-LINK-HERE" ...>

Leave the button style, target, class code, teacher information, and all other recurring content unchanged.

6

Test and publish the duplicate

Use Student View or another student-safe test. Confirm that the green button opens the intended Goblins student page and that the master’s class code remains correct. Verify the page title and Canvas-module placement, then publish the duplicate. Never publish the master template itself.

Before publishing each page

  • The page was duplicated from the correct class-ready master; the master itself remains unpublished.
  • The Canvas page title matches the lesson or assessment code in the planning table.
  • The green button opens the correct student link—not the teacher dashboard.
  • The six-digit class code is correct and includes the hyphen.
  • No placeholder text such as EDIT ME or 000-000 remains.
  • The gray Teacher Setup box has been removed.
  • The item appears in the correct position in the Canvas module.

Daily independent practice provides evidence after each lesson. The midpoint concept check helps teachers identify what is secure and what should be revisited before the module continues. Review Goblins sessions and student reasoning—not only final answers—when planning next steps.

New Student Guide

Welcome to Goblins!

Meet your one-on-one math helper. You will show your thinking, explain your ideas, and get support right when you need it.

Teacher Setup — delete this box before publishing

In the HTML editor, search for EDIT ME. Add your direct Goblins assignment link, class code, teacher name, completion directions, and help link. A direct assignment link gives students the simplest experience.

💡

What is Goblins?

Goblins is an AI-powered math tutor that works alongside your teacher. It watches the math work you choose to share and listens when you explain your reasoning. If you get stuck, it asks helpful questions, draws models, or gives a short mini-lesson. Its job is to help you understand the math—not simply hand you an answer.

🛡️

Use AI with character

Your Goblins conversations and math sessions are monitored and may be reviewed by your teachers. Your teacher can look at your explanations, written work, and conversations to understand how you are thinking and how to help you grow.

Practice responsibility, self-government, and courtesy whenever you speak, draw, or type—even when you are talking with AI. Stay focused on the assignment, use respectful school-appropriate language, and communicate as thoughtfully as you would with a teacher or classmate.

Show your thinking your way

🎙️

Speak

Explain what you notice and why you chose each step.

✏️

Draw

Write equations, label models, and show your work on the math canvas.

⌨️

Type

Type an explanation when speaking or drawing is not the best choice.

Before your first visit

  1. Use a laptop or Chromebook with a reliable internet connection.
  2. Have paper and a pencil nearby if your teacher asks you to use them.
  3. When your browser asks for microphone permission, select Allow if you plan to explain your thinking aloud.
  4. Enter the name or school sign-in your teacher has told you to use. Do not create a second student profile.

How to open your assignment

Always begin on the Canvas page for the lesson you are completing. That page will send you to the correct Goblins work.

1
Click the green Goblins button on your Canvas lesson or assignment page.
2
Sign in only if asked. First-time students may also need the class code shown below.
3
Check the assignment name. It should match the name listed in Canvas. If it does not match, return to Canvas instead of starting a different assignment.
4
Complete every problem and follow the Canvas directions for reporting that you are finished.
Open Goblins in a New Tab
Class code, if requested [EDIT ME: CLASS CODE]

When Goblins asks you a question…

Pause and think before responding. Goblins may ask you to explain a step, try a smaller example, or look at a model. That does not mean you failed—it means the tutor is helping you build the idea.

A strong response sounds like: “I multiplied here because…,” “I notice that…,” “My model shows…,” or “I am confused about this step because…”

Need help?

I do not see the correct assignment
Return to the Canvas lesson and open the Goblins link again. Check the assignment title carefully. If it is still missing, contact your teacher; do not complete a different assignment.
My microphone is not working
Check the microphone symbol near the browser address bar and allow microphone access. Make sure the correct microphone is selected. You may type or draw your thinking while you wait for help.
The page is frozen or will not load
Refresh the page once. If that does not work, close the Goblins tab, return to Canvas, and reopen the assignment link. Check your internet connection before trying again.
I still need help
Contact [EDIT ME: TEACHER NAME] through [EDIT ME: CANVAS INBOX OR HELP LINK]. Include the assignment name and describe what happened.
